translationRepairs: He rose through a series of posts: magistrate of Linhai and Changcheng, staff officer to the Rapid Cavalry General, revising clerk in the Ministry of Works, army aide to the Protector-General, and recorder on the staff of Qi’s Grand Tutor, Prince Ziliang of Jingling.

He rose through a series of posts: magistrate of Linhai and Changcheng, staff officer to the Rapid Cavalry General, revising clerk in the Department of State Affairs, army aide to the Protector-General, and recorder on the staff of Qi’s Minister over the Masses, Prince Ziliang of Jingling.

尚書刪定郎 belongs to the Shangshu (Department of State Affairs), not the Ministry of Works; the proposal’s office fix is right, but 齊司徒 is Minister over the Masses, not Grand Tutor, so the after must correct that remaining error too.

He was promoted in succession to magistrate of Linhai and Changcheng counties, staff officer to the Rapid Cavalry General, revising clerk in the Ministry of Works, army aide to the Protector-General, and recorder on the staff of Prince Ziliang of Jingling, Grand Tutor of Qi.

He was promoted in succession to magistrate of Linhai and Changcheng counties, staff officer to the Rapid Cavalry General, revising clerk in the Department of State Affairs, army aide to the Protector-General, and recorder on the staff of Prince Ziliang of Jingling, Minister over the Masses of Qi.
Same dual error on the literal field: 尚書 is the Shangshu establishment, and 齊司徒 is Minister over the Masses, not Grand Tutor.
His great-grandfather Xuan had been a Jin dynasty recluse-scholar.
His great-great-grandfather Xuan had been a Jin dynasty recluse-scholar.
In the 父/祖/曾祖/高祖 sequence, 高祖 is the fourth ascending generation—great-great-grandfather—not great-grandfather.
His great-grandfather Xuan was a reclusive scholar of Jin.
His great-great-grandfather Xuan was a reclusive scholar of Jin.
Literal likewise: 高祖 denotes great-great-grandfather, so “great-grandfather” undercounts the generation.
Dan served Prince Jingling of Song, Liu Dan; when Dan rebelled, Dan was executed for the crime.
Dan served Prince Jingling of Song, Liu Dan; when the prince rebelled, Dan was executed for the crime.
誕反，淡坐誅 assigns rebellion to 誕 (the prince Liu Dan) and execution to 淡 (Fu Dan); bare “when Dan rebelled, Dan was executed” collapses the two agents.
Grand Tutor Xiu Ren, Prince of Jian’an, heard of this and was delighted; he wished to bring Zhao in, but Zhao, citing the Song court’s turmoil, declined to go.
Liu Xiuren, Prince of Jian’an and Minister over the Masses, heard of this and was delighted; he wished to bring Zhao in, but Zhao, citing the Song court’s turmoil, declined to go.
司徒 is Minister over the Masses (not Grand Tutor/太傅), and 休仁 is the given name Xiuren; “Liu Xiuren, Prince of Jian’an and Minister over the Masses” matches 司徒建安王休仁.
Prince Jian’an, the Grand Tutor Xiu Ren, heard of this and was pleased; he wished to summon Zhao, but Zhao, because the Song house was beset by troubles, did not go.
Prince of Jian’an, Minister over the Masses Xiuren, heard of this and was pleased; he wished to summon Zhao, but Zhao, because the Song house was beset by troubles, did not go.
Literal must likewise render 司徒 as Minister over the Masses and keep 休仁 as Xiuren, not “Grand Tutor Xiu Ren.”
During Qi’s Yongming reign he rose through outer court gentleman, staff officer to Grand Tutor Prince Ziliang of Jingling, and clerk in the Ceremonial Section of the Ministry of Rites.
During Qi’s Yongming reign he rose through outer court gentleman, staff officer to Minister over the Masses Prince Ziliang of Jingling, and clerk in the Ceremonial Section of the Ministry of Rites.
司徒竟陵王子良 names Ziliang as Minister over the Masses; Grand Tutor would be 太傅.
In Qi’s Yongming era he was promoted in succession to outer court gentleman, staff officer to the Grand Tutor Prince Ziliang of Jingling, and clerk in the Ministry of Rites’ Ceremonial Section.

In Qi’s Yongming era he was promoted in succession to outer court gentleman, staff officer to the Minister over the Masses Prince Ziliang of Jingling, and clerk in the Ministry of Rites’ Ceremonial Section.
Same 司徒/Grand Tutor mistranslation on the literal field; Minister over the Masses is the correct office.

In year 6 he was transferred to Minister of the Left People; before taking the seal he was sent out as General Who Establishes Might, chief clerk to the Pacification Prince of Ancheng, and administrator of Xunyang.

In year 6 he was transferred to Minister of the Left People; before taking the seal he was sent out as General Who Establishes Might, chief clerk to the Prince of Ancheng (General Who Pacifies the South), and administrator of Xunyang.
平南安成王長史 is chief clerk to the Prince of Ancheng who held the generalship 平南, not a fused title “Pacification Prince.”

In the sixth year he was moved to Minister of the Left People; before he received the seal he went out as General Who Establishes Might, chief clerk to the Pacification Prince of Ancheng, and Administrator of Xunyang.

In the sixth year he was moved to Minister of the Left People; before he received the seal he went out as General Who Establishes Might, chief clerk to the Prince of Ancheng, General Who Pacifies the South, and Administrator of Xunyang.
Literal likewise must split 平南 as General Who Pacifies the South from the princely title 安成王.
In year 12 he returned as Director of the Secretariat and concurrently commanded the Rear Army General.
In year 12 he returned as Director of the Secretariat and concurrently held appointment as General of the Rear Army.
領後軍將軍 means concurrent tenure of the Rear Army generalship, not commanding another person titled Rear Army General.
His eldest son Xu served as a gentleman of the Ministry of Works and as magistrate of Lin’an.
His eldest son Xu served as a gentleman of the Masters of Writing and as magistrate of Lin’an.
尚書郎 is a gentleman of the Masters of Writing/Shangshu, not an officer of the Ministry of Works (工部).
His eldest son Xu was a gentleman of the Ministry of Works and magistrate of Lin’an.
His eldest son Xu was a gentleman of the Masters of Writing and magistrate of Lin’an.
Same office mistranslation on the literal field: 尚書郎 is Masters of Writing, not Ministry of Works.

When Zhao first took office at Linhai, Lu Chun gave him a farewell feast; host and guests made merry until dusk, and Zhao did not return. Ying thought his elder brother, at his age, should not carouse all night; he went to fetch him himself, and they rode home together—both already gray-haired. Contemporaries admired and revered the deed.

When Zhao first took office at Linhai, Lu Chui gave him a farewell feast; host and guests made merry until dusk, and Zhao did not return. Ying thought his elder brother, at his age, should not carouse all night; he went to fetch him himself, and they rode home together—both already gray-haired. Contemporaries admired and revered the deed.
陸倕 is Lu Chui (倕 Chuí); Chun misreads the given name.

When Zhao first became administrator of Linhai, Lu Chun gave him a farewell feast; host and guests were all merry, and at dusk he did not return. Ying thought that Zhao, being advanced in years, ought not to revel through the night to excess, and so went himself to meet him; they rode back together. Both brothers’ hair was already streaked with white, and people of the time admired and submitted to this.

When Zhao first became administrator of Linhai, Lu Chui gave him a farewell feast; host and guests were all merry, and at dusk he did not return. Ying thought that Zhao, being advanced in years, ought not to revel through the night to excess, and so went himself to meet him; they rode back together. Both brothers’ hair was already streaked with white, and people of the time admired and submitted to this.
Literal likewise must render 陸倕 as Lu Chui, not Lu Chun.

He later served as recording officer to the Prince of Linchuan, drafter for the Southern Office, recording officer to the Prince of Ancheng, and Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard, rising through Palace Gentleman, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, and Grand Master of the Palace.

He later served as recording officer to the Prince of Linchuan, drafter for the Southern Office, recording officer to the Prince of Ancheng, and Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard, rising through Palace Gentleman, Chamberlain for Ceremonials, and Grand Master of the Palace.
光祿卿 is Chamberlain for Ceremonials; Grand Master of Splendid Happiness is 光祿大夫, a different office.

He again served as recording officer on the staff of the Prince of Linchuan, drafting documents for the Southern Office, recording officer to the Prince of Ancheng, and Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard; he was promoted in succession to Palace Gentleman, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, and Grand Master of the Palace.

He again served as recording officer on the staff of the Prince of Linchuan, drafting documents for the Southern Office, recording officer to the Prince of Ancheng, and Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Guard; he was promoted in succession to Palace Gentleman, Chamberlain for Ceremonials, and Grand Master of the Palace.
Same 光祿卿/光祿大夫 confusion on the literal field; Chamberlain for Ceremonials is correct.
On this embassy he presented the book to Prince Fan of Poyang, who in turn offered it to the Eastern Palace.
On this journey he presented the book to Prince Fan of Poyang, who in turn offered it to the Eastern Palace.
及是行也 means on this journey/trip; “embassy” invents a diplomatic mission type absent from the Chinese.
In year 15 he was made Left Chief Clerk of the Grand Tutor.
In year 15 he was made Left Chief Clerk to the Minister over the Masses.
司徒左長史 is Left Chief Clerk to the Minister over the Masses; Grand Tutor would be 太傅.
In the fifteenth year he was transferred to Left Chief Clerk of the Grand Tutor.
In the fifteenth year he was transferred to Left Chief Clerk of the Minister over the Masses.
Literal likewise: 司徒 is Minister over the Masses, not Grand Tutor.

Zhang Ji, the Army Director, was Gao’s maternal uncle; Gao once impeached him on official grounds. At a banquet Ji complained to the High Ancestor: “Lu Gao is my close kinsman by marriage—over a trifle he impeached me and would show no mercy.”

Zhang Ji, the Army Director, was Gao’s collateral maternal uncle; Gao once impeached him on official grounds. At a banquet Ji complained to the High Ancestor: “Lu Gao is my close kinsman—over a trifle he impeached me and would show no mercy.”
從舅 is a collateral maternal uncle, not simply maternal uncle (舅); 通親 means close kinsman, without “by marriage.”

The Army Director Zhang Ji was Gao’s maternal uncle; Gao once impeached Ji on public grounds. At a banquet Ji complained to the High Ancestor, saying, “Lu Gao is my close kin by marriage; on a trifling matter he impeached me and would not spare me.”

Literal must likewise render 從舅 as collateral maternal uncle and 通親 as close kin without inventing marriage.
